1	# Plan d'implémentation : S-02b (DEVDESK-711) — arrêt propre d'abord (Linux, macOS), puis forcer sur confirmation
2	
3	Une seule PR, branche `feat/safe-process-stop-s02b`, base `origin/main` ec457184 (S-01a, S-02a, S-01b, bug 714 fusionnés).
4	Spécification : `docs/product/safe-process-stop/stories.md`, S-02b (7 critères, contrainte Rule 110 / tick ~250 ms / génération). Non rediscutée.
5	Plans précédents : `DEVDESK-708-plan.md` (seams, `realOS.kill`, `pendingKill`), `DEVDESK-709-plan.md` (`Identity`, `ConfirmIdentity`, `refusal`, `targetPresence`).
6	
7	## 0. Ce que dit le code aujourd'hui (lu le 2026-11-23, `main` ec457184)
8	
9	- `internal/ports/procos.go` : seams `selfPID`, `parentPID`, `goos`, `now`, `procOS osProcs = realOS{}`. `osProcs` = `createTime`, `identity(pid) (uint64, error)`, `kill(pid, want Identity) error`. `realOS.kill` : `refuseRealSignalUnderTest` (1re instruction) → `os.FindProcess` (pidfd Linux ≥ 5.4, handle Windows) → `heldIdentity` → `verdictAtSignal` → `p.Kill()`.
10	- `internal/ports/ports.go` : `Kill(pid string, listed Identity) error` = `parsePID` → `protectionOf` → `n <= 0` → identité connue sinon `*UnverifiableError` → `procOS.kill` enveloppé `killing process N: %w`.
11	- `internal/ports/identity.go` : `parseStartTicks` (champs comptés après la dernière `)`), `verdictAtSignal`, `ConfirmIdentity`. Lecteurs par OS : `identity_{linux,darwin,windows,other}.go` (`readIdentity`, `heldIdentity`, `isNoSuchProcess`). macOS lit `unix.SysctlKinfoProc("kern.proc.pid", pid)`.
12	- `internal/ports/signal_guard_test.go` : `TestOnlyRealOSSendsASignal` refuse `FindProcess`, `Kill`, `Signal`, `TerminateProcess` (nom du sélecteur) hors de `(realOS) kill`, dont la 1re instruction doit être `refuseRealSignalUnderTest`.
13	- `internal/ui/netdiag/ports_commands.go` : `processOps{protection, confirm, kill, windows}`, `killProcessCmd(kill, t)`, `portsRefreshMsg`, `requestPortsRefresh()`.
14	- `internal/ui/netdiag/ports_model.go` (679 lignes) : `confirmKill` (gardes → `ops.confirm` → `pendingKill` → modale `Kill Process` / `killPrompt`), `handleConfirmYes` (`targetPresence` → protection → busy → `MarkBusy("Killing …")` → `killProcessCmd`), `handleKillResult` (`ClearBusy`, `refusal`, Info `Process N terminated`), `refusal` (classement unique), `killable()` (ligne → PID → protection → identité), `killPrompt(t, windows)`, `killHelpDescription(windows)`. `esc` n'a aucun rôle sur l'onglet Ports aujourd'hui (`handleKeyNormal` ne le traite pas ; la modale le traduit en `ConfirmModalNoMsg`).
15	- `internal/ui/netdiag/update.go` : les messages Ports sont aiguillés par type (`case portsTickMsg, portsDataMsg, portsKillResultMsg, portsRefreshMsg`), quel que soit l'onglet actif ; `jobs.FrameMsg` pousse la phase de clignotement au tableau Ports ; `routeConfirm` envoie Yes/No à Forward si l'onglet actif est Forward, sinon à Ports.
16	- `internal/ui/netdiag/ports_activity.go` : `WantsBlink()` vrai tant qu'une marque busy existe (le point de la ligne clignote).
17	- `internal/ui/netdiag/header.go` : `K` « Kill process » (grisé par `killable()`), aide « Ports Tab — How it works » et `killHelpDescription`.
18	- `internal/ui/netdiag/view.go` : la modale Ports est posée par `lipgloss.Place` ; `ConfirmModal.View()` ne replie pas les lignes (padding 2 + bordure 1 de chaque côté).
19	- **Routeur** (`internal/app/app.go`) : un message non reconnu va à la vue **active** (`forwardToActiveView`). Si l'utilisateur quitte `:net` pendant un kill, `portsKillResultMsg` est perdu et la ligne reste busy (défaut existant, non signalé) ; `routeToView` existe pour router vers une vue hors écran. `Running()` de netdiag protège la vue d'une suppression (`command_line.go:161`).
20	- Aucun appelant de `ports.Kill` hors de netdiag ; le MCP (`internal/mcp/ports_tools.go`) n'appelle que `ports.List`.
21	
22	Vérifié dans les sources :
23	- Go 1.27.4 `os/exec_unix.go` : `(*Process).signal` passe par `pidfdSendSignal` quand un pidfd est tenu, sinon `kill(2)` ; `p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM)` bénéficie donc de la même garantie « processus tenu » que `p.Kill()`. `ESRCH` → `os.ErrProcessDone`, `EPERM` → `errors.Is(err, os.ErrPermission)`.
24	- `syscall.SIGTERM` existe sous Windows (`syscall/types_windows.go`) : `realOS.kill` compile partout ; `os.Process.Signal` y rend une erreur « not supported », jamais atteinte (section 3.2).
25	- `golang.org/x/sys v0.49.0` darwin : `KinfoProc.Proc.P_stat int8` existe ; **aucune constante `SZOMB` exportée** → constante locale `darwinSZOMB = 5` (`<sys/proc.h>` : SIDL 1, SRUN 2, SSLEEP 3, SSTOP 4, SZOMB 5).
26	- `testutil.FastTimers(t, *time.Duration)` ramène une durée à 1 ms pour un test.
27	
28	## 1. Exigences non fonctionnelles
29	
30	- **Sûreté** : jamais de SIGKILL sans la seconde confirmation (critère 3). Chaque signal (SIGTERM puis SIGKILL) passe par le même `realOS.kill`, processus tenu, avec la même vérification d'identité contre l'identité capturée à la confirmation (critère 5). La sonde n'envoie **aucun** signal (pas même le signal 0).
31	- **Réactivité (Rule 110)** : aucune attente bloquante ; l'attente est une chaîne de `tea.Tick` (250 ms) dont chaque tick sonde et renvoie un message portant une génération ; seul `Update` modifie le modèle.
32	- **Coût** : au plus ~21 sondes par arrêt (une lecture de `/proc/<pid>/stat` sous Linux, un `sysctl` sous macOS) ; aucune lecture au rendu.
33	- **Portabilité** : `GOOS=linux|darwin|windows` compilent, `go vet` et `go test -c` passent pour les trois. Windows : comportement S-02a **inchangé**.
34	- **Exploitabilité** : logs `log.Printf("ERROR [netdiag/ports] …")` pour une sonde illisible ; `INFO` quand un zombie est compté arrêté.
35	- **Tests sans vrai signal** : tout par seams ; vrais signaux seulement sur des enfants lancés par le test (`allowRealSignals`), Linux.
36	
37	## 2. Options comparées
38	
39	### 2.1 Où vit l'attente
40	
41	| Option | Pour | Contre |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| A. Dans `internal/ports` : `StopGracefully(pid, id, 5s)` bloquant dans un `Cmd` | Une seule fonction | Un `Cmd` qui dort 5 s : `esc` ne peut pas l'interrompre sans contexte, la seconde confirmation est un état UI, la génération perd son sens ; contraire à la contrainte de conception |
44	| **B. Machine à états dans `netdiag`, primitives sans état dans `ports` (recommandée)** : `ports.Terminate`, `ports.Probe`, `ports.Kill` ; le modèle tient l'arrêt en cours, une chaîne de ticks sonde | Conforme à la contrainte (tick + sonde + génération) ; chaque primitive testable seule ; `ports` ne connaît ni l'UI ni le temps | Plus de messages côté UI |
45	
46	### 2.2 Envoyer SIGTERM
47	
48	| Option | Pour | Contre |
49	|---|---|---|
50	| **A. `realOS.kill(pid, want, sig)` reçoit le signal à envoyer (recommandée)** | Un seul point d'envoi, une seule vérification d'identité pour les deux signaux (critère 5) ; le garde statique et le garde à l'exécution restent **inchangés** (`p.Signal` et `p.Kill` dans `(realOS) kill`) | La méthode s'appelle toujours `kill` alors qu'elle peut envoyer SIGTERM (commentaire) |
51	| B. Une seconde méthode `realOS.term` | Nom exact | Deux points d'envoi : il faut changer `TestOnlyRealOSSendsASignal` (deux méthodes autorisées, deux gardes en tête) et dupliquer `FindProcess` + vérification ; le risque qu'une seule des deux vérifie grandit |
52	
53	### 2.3 Sonde « vivant / zombie / sorti »
54	
55	| Option | Pour | Contre |
56	|---|---|---|
57	| A. `kill(pid, 0)` / `p.Signal(0)` | Classique | Un signal (même nul) : le garde le refuse hors `realOS.kill` ; ne distingue pas le zombie (signal 0 réussit sur un zombie) ; ne voit pas un PID repris |
58	| B. Interroger le pidfd (`poll`) | Exact sous Linux ≥ 5.4 | Il faudrait tenir le pidfd pendant 5 s entre deux `Cmd` (état système hors modèle) ; rien sous macOS |
59	| **C. Lecture d'état sans signal, par PID, comparée à l'identité (recommandée)** : Linux `/proc/<pid>/stat` (état champ 3 + `starttime` champ 22 en une lecture) ; macOS `kinfo_proc` (`P_stat`, `P_starttime`) | Aucun signal ; détecte zombie **et** PID repris (identité différente = le processus visé est parti) ; réutilise `parseStartTicks` et le lecteur macOS existants | Une lecture par sonde ; macOS non exécuté en CI |
60	
61	### 2.4 Messages quand l'utilisateur quitte `:net`
62	
63	| Option | Pour | Contre |
64	|---|---|---|
65	| A. Rien : messages perdus hors écran | Aucun changement du routeur | L'arrêt reste « en attente » pour toujours → `K` grisé `Another stop is already in progress` à vie (critère 7 faux) ; la ligne reste busy |
66	| B. Réarmer dans `Init` au retour | Local à netdiag | Le résultat du SIGTERM perdu est inconnaissable (envoyé ou refusé ?) ; un tick réarmé peut doubler la chaîne |
67	| **C. 94	- **Un seul arrêt en attente** : `pm.stop *pendingStop` (nil = aucun). Phases `signalling`, `waiting`, `askingForce`, `forcing`. `pendingKill` reste la cible de la **première** confirmation (inchangé, Windows inclus).
95	- **Génération** : chaque arrêt reçoit `gen = nextStopGen()` (compteur `atomic.Uint64` de paquet, unique même entre deux modèles netdiag reconstruits). Tout message d'arrêt dont `gen` ≠ `pm.stop.gen`, ou reçu quand `pm.stop == nil`, ou dans une phase qui ne l'attend pas, est **ignoré** sans effet. `esc` met `pm.stop = nil` : le tick en vol devient périmé ; un nouvel arrêt lancé aussitôt a une autre génération, donc l'ancien tick ne le touche pas.
96	- **Échéance** : `deadline = msg.at + stopGrace`, `at` étant l'instant où le `Cmd` du SIGTERM a rendu ; chaque `portsStopProbeMsg` porte l'instant du tick (`tea.Tick` le fournit). Aucune horloge dans le modèle : les tests fixent `at`.
97	- **Sonde illisible** (erreur autre que « parti ») : journalisée, comptée **vivante** (aucune fausse annonce « stopped ») ; l'échéance amène la seconde confirmation, dont le SIGKILL revérifie l'identité.
98	- **Seconde étape** (`Yes`) : `targetPresence(target)` → `replaced` : `refusal(IdentityChangedError)` (critère 5, sans appel système) ; `absent` **n'arrête pas** la seconde étape (un processus qui s'arrête ferme souvent ses sockets avant de sortir ; c'est le cas même que la seconde étape doit traiter — l'identité est revérifiée au signal) ; protection recalculée ; puis SIGKILL par `pm.ops.kill(pid, target.Identity)`.
99	- **Résultat du SIGKILL d'un arrêt en deux temps** : `os.ErrProcessDone` → Info `x (N) stopped` (le processus est sorti de lui-même entre l'échéance et `Yes` ; décision proposée, plus juste que l'Error `PID N is no longer running`) ; `IdentityChangedError` → texte S-01b critère 2 + relecture (critère 5) ; le reste par `refusal` ; succès → Info `Process N terminated` (inchangé).
100	- **Pendant l'attente** : le tableau continue de se rafraîchir (chaîne `portsTickMsg` indépendante, la pause `space` reste un choix de l'utilisateur), toutes les touches répondent ; la chaîne de sonde n'est pas suspendue quand le terminal perd le focus (5 s bornées).
101	- **Windows** : `pm.stop` n'est **jamais** posé. `handleConfirmYes` garde exactement le chemin S-02a (`MarkBusy("Killing …")` + `killProcessCmd(kill, t, 0)`), sélectionné par `pm.ops.windows` (lui-même `runtime.GOOS == "windows"` en production, injecté en test). Aucune attente, aucune seconde confirmation, aucun texte nouveau.

335	
336	- **Rule 110** : `terminateCmd`, `stopProbeCmd`, `killProcessCmd` ne lisent pas le modèle ; toutes les transitions sont dans `Update`.
337	- **Rule 130** : la liste des raccourcis d'un même écran ne change pas d'un état à l'autre (`esc` toujours présent sous Unix, grisé hors attente). `K` grisé pendant un arrêt est une **exception assumée** à « une opération en cours n'est pas une cause de grisé » : imposée par le critère 7, l'état dure au plus 5 s puis une modale, et la raison s'affiche à l'appui (Warn). À écrire dans D176 et `network.md`. `esc` est un contrôle : grisé suffit, pas de pied de page à l'appui hors attente.
338	- **Rule 128** : niveaux — fin, annulation, refus de forcer : Info ; grisé : Warn ; refus du système : Error. 80 colonnes : `FooterMessage` tronque ; à 80 colonnes, chaque texte du critère est complet pour `nginx (812)`. 349	| `ProtectionOf` / `protectionOf` | Inchangés ; évalués dans `Kill` et `Terminate` (préambule commun) et recalculés aux deux `Yes`. |
350	| Relecture du tableau | `requestPortsRefresh()` après un arrêt réussi (la ligne disparaît sans attendre 2 s), même en pause (précédent D175 Q3) ; refus d'identité : inchangé. La chaîne `portsTickMsg` n'est pas touchée. |
351	| MCP | Aucun changement : il n'expose que `ports.List`. |
352	| Routeur | `BackgroundMsg` routé vers netdiag (3.3) ; corrige aussi la ligne busy perdue d'un kill quand on quitte `:net`. |
353	
354	## 4. Étapes
355	
356	Graphe : **1 → 2 → {3 ∥ 4} → {5 ∥ 6} → 7**. Les étapes 1 et 2 touchent la même interface `osProcs` et le même `fakeOS` : séquentielles. 3 (tests réels `ports`) et 4 (UI) sont parallélisables. 5 (en-tête, aide, libellés) et 6 (routeur) sont parallélisables. Chaque étape laisse `go build ./...` et `go test ./internal/ports/ ./internal/ui/netdiag/ ./internal/app/` verts.
357	
358	---
359	
360	### Étape 1 — `internal/ports` : `realOS.kill` reçoit le signal, `Terminate` (critères 1, 5, 6 côté `ports`)
361	
362	**Fichiers.** `procos.go` (`stopSignal`, `osProcs.kill(pid, want, sig)`, `realOS.kill`), `ports.go` (`signalTarget`, `Kill` via `signalKill`, `Terminate`, `ErrNoCleanStop`), `seams_test.go` (`fakeOS.kill` enregistre `sigs []stopSignal`), `signal_guard_test.go` et `identity_kill_test.go` / `kill_test.go` (appels `realOS{}.kill(…, signalKill)`). Nouveau `terminate_test.go`.
363	
364	**Tests rouges d'abord.**
365	- `TestTerminateSendsSIGTERMWithTheListedIdentity` : `useFakeOS(t, 100, 99, "linux")`, `Terminate("4242", IdentityForTest(9))` → `nil`, `fake.kills == [4242]`, `fake.sigs == [signalTerm]`, `fake.killedWith == [IdentityForTest(9)]`.
366	- `TestKillStillSendsSIGKILL` : `Kill("4242", IdentityForTest(9))` → `fake.sigs == [signalKill]`.
367	- `TestTerminateRefusesLikeKill` (table, `linux`) : self `100` → `*ProtectedError` ; `1` → `*ProtectedError` ; `Identity{}` → `*UnverifiableError` avec le texte S-01b ; `DeferredIdentityForTest` → `*UnverifiableError` ; `"abc"`, `"0"` → `not a process id` ; aucune entrée dans `fake.kills`.
368	- `TestTerminateOnWindowsHasNoCleanStop` : `goos = "windows"`, `Terminate("4412", IdentityForTest(1))` → `errors.Is(err, ErrNoCleanStop)`, aucun appel ; `Terminate("4", …)` → `*ProtectedError` (la protection d'abord).
369	- `TestTerminateKeepsTheOSErrorReadable` : `killErr = os.ErrPermission` / `os.ErrProcessDone` → `errors.Is` vrai à travers `stopping process N: %w`.
370	- `TestANamelessSignalIsRefused` : `recoverPanic` n'est pas en jeu ; avec `allowRealSignals(t)` et `unreachablePID`, `realOS{}.kill(unreachablePID, IdentityForTest(1), 0)` → erreur `no signal named`, sans signal (le PID n'existe pas de toute façon).
371	- Gardes : `TestARealSignalInATestBinaryPanics` gagne un sous-cas `signalTerm` ; nouveau `TestTerminateWithoutASubstitutedProcOSHitsTheGuard` ; `TestOnlyRealOSSendsASignal` vert **sans modification**.
372	
373	**Commandes.**
374	```
375	go test ./internal/ports/ -count=1
376	GOOS=windows go vet ./internal/ports/ && GOOS=darwin go vet ./internal/ports/
377	GOOS=windows go test -c -o /dev/null ./internal/ports/ && GOOS=darwin go test -c -o /dev/null ./internal/ports/
378	```
379	**Critère de fin.** Tests verts ; `Kill` inchangé pour ses appelants ; garde statique inchangé et vert.
380	**Dépendances.** Aucune.

384	### Étape 2 — `internal/ports` : `Probe` et lecture d'état par OS (critère 2 côté `ports`)
385	
386	**Fichiers.** `identity.go` (`parseStat`, `parseStartTicks` réécrit dessus, `isLinuxZombie`, `darwinSZOMB`, `isDarwinZombie`, `livenessOf`), `identity_linux.go` / `identity_darwin.go` (`readStatus`, `readIdentity` dessus), `identity_windows.go` / `identity_other.go` (`readStatus` → `errors.ErrUnsupported`), `procos.go` (`procStatus`, `osProcs.probe`, `realOS.probe`), nouveau `probe.go` (`Liveness`, `Stopped`, `String`, `Probe`), `seams_test.go` (`fakeOS.status map[int]procStatus`, `statusErr map[int]error`, `probeCalls []int`). Nouveau `probe_test.go`.
387	
388	**Tests rouges d'abord.**
389	- `TestParseStat` (table) : ligne réelle → état `S` et `starttime` ; `comm` = `a) (b c)` → bons champs ; état `Z` ; ligne tronquée avant le champ 22 → erreur ; vide → erreur. `TestParseStartTicks` existant vert sans changement.
390	- `TestZombieStates` : `isLinuxZombie('Z')`, `('X')` vrais ; `'S'`, `'R'`, `'D'`, `'T'` faux ; `isDarwinZombie(5)` vrai, `(2)`, `(3)` faux.

393	- `TestProbeReadsOnceAndSendsNothing` : `Probe("812", IdentityForTest(7))` → `probeCalls == [812]`, `fake.kills` vide.
394	- `TestStoppedCountsZombieAndExited` : `ProcessRunning.Stopped() == false`, les deux autres vrais.

397	**Commandes.** Celles de l'étape 1, plus `go test ./internal/ports/ -count=1 -run 'ParseStat|Zombie|Liveness|Probe|RealStatus'`.
398	**Critère de fin.** Tests verts ; compilation croisée des tests ; garde statique vert (aucun nom de signal dans les lecteurs).
399	**Dépendances.** Étape 1.

404	
405	**Fichiers.** Nouveau `stop_real_test.go` (Linux ; `t.Skip` ailleurs). Processus auxiliaires dans le binaire de test : `TestHelperProcessSleeps` (existant), nouveaux `TestHelperProcessIgnoresTerm` (`signal.Ignore(syscall.SIGTERM)`, écrit `ready\n` sur stdout puis dort) et `TestHelperProcessExits` (sort aussitôt). Chaque test lit l'identité par `realOS{}.identity(pid)`, appelle `allowRealSignals(t)` seulement s'il signale, et `Wait()` en `t.Cleanup`.
406	
407	**Tests rouges d'abord.**
408	- `TestTerminateEndsARealChildProcess` : enfant `Sleeps`, `Terminate(pid, id)` → `nil` ; l'enfant se termine dans 2 s ; `cmd.ProcessState` dit « signal: terminated ».
409	- `TestTerminateSparesARealChildWhoseIdentityDiffers` (critère 5 pour SIGTERM) : `Terminate(pid, IdentityForTest(raw+1))` → `*IdentityChangedError` ; 300 ms plus tard l'enfant tourne toujours.
410	- `TestProbeSeesARealZombie` (critère 2, **sans signal**) : enfant `Exits`, sans `Wait` ; sonder jusqu'à 2 s → `ProcessZombie` ; après `Wait` → `ProcessExited`.

417	go test -race ./internal/ports/ -count=2
418	```

422	---
423	
424	### Étape 4 — `internal/ui/netdiag` : la machine à états (critères 1 à 7)
425	
426	**Fichiers.** Nouveau `ports_stop.go` (3.3) ; `ports_commands.go` (`processOps.terminate/probe`, `realProcessOps`, `terminateCmd`, `stopProbeCmd`, `killProcessCmd(…, gen)`) ; `ports_model.go` (`stop`, `update`, `handleKeyNormal` esc, `killable`, `handleConfirmYes`, `handleKillResult`, `killPrompt` Unix) ; `update.go` (case des messages, `Running`) ; `ports_target_test.go` (`fakeProcs` : `terminated []string`, `termErr error`, `probed []string`, `probeAnswer map[string]ports.Liveness`, `probeErr error` ; `ops` câble `terminate` et `probe`) ; nouveau `ports_stop_test.go`. Adapter les tests existants dont la 1re `Yes` Unix attend `Killing …` ou un `kill` (ils voient désormais `Stopping …` et un `terminate`) : `ports_footer_test.go` (`killingSSHD`), `ports_target_test.go` (`TestYesKillsTheCapturedTargetAfterTheTableReorders`, `TestUnixConfirmationIsUnchanged` → remplacé à l'étape 5), `ports_identity_test.go`, `ports_protect_test.go` (vérifier chaque assertion `killed` sous Unix : elle devient `terminated`). Les tests Windows ne changent pas.
427	
428	Convention : `testutil.FastTimers(t, &components.FooterMsgDuration)` en 1re ligne de tout test qui exécute un `Cmd` ; les ticks de sonde ne sont **pas** exécutés (on fabrique `portsStopProbeMsg` avec `gen` lu dans `pm.stop.gen` et `at` choisi), sauf le test Rule 110 qui raccourcit `stopProbeEvery`.

430	**Tests rouges d'abord** (`t0` = `at` du résultat SIGTERM injecté).
431	1. `TestTheStopConfirmationAnnouncesTwoSteps` (crit. 1) : Unix, `K` sur `nginx` 812 → titre `Stop Process` ; `squash(body) == "Ask nginx (PID 812) to stop? Sends SIGTERM and waits up to 5 s. You can force it afterwards."` ; le corps ne contient pas `SIGKILL`.

436	6. `TestStillRunningBeforeTheDeadlineProbesAgain` : `{t0+4750ms, ProcessRunning}` → toujours `stopWaiting`, `Cmd` non nul, aucune modale.
437	7. `TestStillRunningAtTheDeadlineAsksToForce` (crit. 3) : `{t0+5s, ProcessRunning}` → phase `stopAskingForce`, titre `Force Kill`, `squash(body) == "nginx (PID 812) did not exit within 5 s. Force kill (SIGKILL)? It gets no chance to shut down cleanly."`, busy levé, `killed` vide.

1	# Plan d'implémentation : S-02b (DEVDESK-711) — arrêt propre d'abord (Linux, macOS), puis forcer sur confirmation
2	
3	Une seule PR, branche `feat/safe-process-stop-s02b`, base `origin/main` ec457184 (S-01a, S-02a, S-01b, bug 714 fusionnés).
4	Spécification : `docs/product/safe-process-stop/stories.md`, S-02b (7 critères, contrainte Rule 110 / tick ~250 ms / génération). Non rediscutée.
5	Plans précédents : `DEVDESK-708-plan.md` (seams, `realOS.kill`, `pendingKill`), `DEVDESK-709-plan.md` (`Identity`, `ConfirmIdentity`, `refusal`, `targetPresence`).
6	
7	## 0. Ce que dit le code aujourd'hui (lu le 2026-11-23, `main` ec457184)
8	
9	- `internal/ports/procos.go` : seams `selfPID`, `parentPID`, `goos`, `now`, `procOS osProcs = realOS{}`. `osProcs` = `createTime`, `identity(pid) (uint64, error)`, `kill(pid, want Identity) error`. `realOS.kill` : `refuseRealSignalUnderTest` (1re instruction) → `os.FindProcess` (pidfd Linux ≥ 5.4, handle Windows) → `heldIdentity` → `verdictAtSignal` → `p.Kill()`.
10	- `internal/ports/ports.go` : `Kill(pid string, listed Identity) error` = `parsePID` → `protectionOf` → `n <= 0` → identité connue sinon `*UnverifiableError` → `procOS.kill` enveloppé `killing process N: %w`.
11	- `internal/ports/identity.go` : `parseStartTicks` (champs comptés après la dernière `)`), `verdictAtSignal`, `ConfirmIdentity`. Lecteurs par OS : `identity_{linux,darwin,windows,other}.go` (`readIdentity`, `heldIdentity`, `isNoSuchProcess`). macOS lit `unix.SysctlKinfoProc("kern.proc.pid", pid)`.
12	- `internal/ports/signal_guard_test.go` : `TestOnlyRealOSSendsASignal` refuse `FindProcess`, `Kill`, `Signal`, `TerminateProcess` (nom du sélecteur) hors de `(realOS) kill`, dont la 1re instruction doit être `refuseRealSignalUnderTest`.
13	- `internal/ui/netdiag/ports_commands.go` : `processOps{protection, confirm, kill, windows}`, `killProcessCmd(kill, t)`, `portsRefreshMsg`, `requestPortsRefresh()`.
14	- `internal/ui/netdiag/ports_model.go` (679 lignes) : `confirmKill` (gardes → `ops.confirm` → `pendingKill` → modale `Kill Process` / `killPrompt`), `handleConfirmYes` (`targetPresence` → protection → busy → `MarkBusy("Killing …")` → `killProcessCmd`), `handleKillResult` (`ClearBusy`, `refusal`, Info `Process N terminated`), `refusal` (classement unique), `killable()` (ligne → PID → protection → identité), `killPrompt(t, windows)`, `killHelpDescription(windows)`. `esc` n'a aucun rôle sur l'onglet Ports aujourd'hui (`handleKeyNormal` ne le traite pas ; la modale le traduit en `ConfirmModalNoMsg`).
15	- `internal/ui/netdiag/update.go` : les messages Ports sont aiguillés par type (`case portsTickMsg, portsDataMsg, portsKillResultMsg, portsRefreshMsg`), quel que soit l'onglet actif ; `jobs.FrameMsg` pousse la phase de clignotement au tableau Ports ; `routeConfirm` envoie Yes/No à Forward si l'onglet actif est Forward, sinon à Ports.
16	- `internal/ui/netdiag/ports_activity.go` : `WantsBlink()` vrai tant qu'une marque busy existe (le point de la ligne clignote).
17	- `internal/ui/netdiag/header.go` : `K` « Kill process » (grisé par `killable()`), aide « Ports Tab — How it works » et `killHelpDescription`.
18	- `internal/ui/netdiag/view.go` : la modale Ports est posée par `lipgloss.Place` ; `ConfirmModal.View()` ne replie pas les lignes (padding 2 + bordure 1 de chaque côté).
19	- **Routeur** (`internal/app/app.go`) : un message non reconnu va à la vue **active** (`forwardToActiveView`). Si l'utilisateur quitte `:net` pendant un kill, `portsKillResultMsg` est perdu et la ligne reste busy (défaut existant, non signalé) ; `routeToView` existe pour router vers une vue hors écran. `Running()` de netdiag protège la vue d'une suppression (`command_line.go:161`).
20	- Aucun appelant de `ports.Kill` hors de netdiag ; le MCP (`internal/mcp/ports_tools.go`) n'appelle que `ports.List`.
21	
22	Vérifié dans les sources :
23	- Go 1.27.4 `os/exec_unix.go` : `(*Process).signal` passe par `pidfdSendSignal` quand un pidfd est tenu, sinon `kill(2)` ; `p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM)` bénéficie donc de la même garantie « processus tenu » que `p.Kill()`. `ESRCH` → `os.ErrProcessDone`, `EPERM` → `errors.Is(err, os.ErrPermission)`.
24	- `syscall.SIGTERM` existe sous Windows (`syscall/types_windows.go`) : `realOS.kill` compile partout ; `os.Process.Signal` y rend une erreur « not supported », jamais atteinte (section 3.2).
25	- `golang.org/x/sys v0.49.0` darwin : `KinfoProc.Proc.P_stat int8` existe ; **aucune constante `SZOMB` exportée** → constante locale `darwinSZOMB = 5` (`<sys/proc.h>` : SIDL 1, SRUN 2, SSLEEP 3, SSTOP 4, SZOMB 5).
26	- `testutil.FastTimers(t, *time.Duration)` ramène une durée à 1 ms pour un test.
27	
28	## 1. Exigences non fonctionnelles
29	
30	- **Sûreté** : jamais de SIGKILL sans la seconde confirmation (critère 3). Chaque signal (SIGTERM puis SIGKILL) passe par le même `realOS.kill`, processus tenu, avec la même vérification d'identité contre l'identité capturée à la confirmation (critère 5). La sonde n'envoie **aucun** signal (pas même le signal 0).
31	- **Réactivité (Rule 110)** : aucune attente bloquante ; l'attente est une chaîne de `tea.Tick` (250 ms) dont chaque tick sonde et renvoie un message portant une génération ; seul `Update` modifie le modèle.
32	- **Coût** : au plus ~21 sondes par arrêt (une lecture de `/proc/<pid>/stat` sous Linux, un `sysctl` sous macOS) ; aucune lecture au rendu.
33	- **Portabilité** : `GOOS=linux|darwin|windows` compilent, `go vet` et `go test -c` passent pour les trois. Windows : comportement S-02a **inchangé**.
34	- **Exploitabilité** : logs `log.Printf("ERROR [netdiag/ports] …")` pour une sonde illisible ; `INFO` quand un zombie est compté arrêté.
35	- **Tests sans vrai signal** : tout par seams ; vrais signaux seulement sur des enfants lancés par le test (`allowRealSignals`), Linux.
36	
37	## 2. Options comparées
38	
39	### 2.1 Où vit l'attente
40	
41	| Option | Pour | Contre |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| A. Dans `internal/ports` : `StopGracefully(pid, id, 5s)` bloquant dans un `Cmd` | Une seule fonction | Un `Cmd` qui dort 5 s : `esc` ne peut pas l'interrompre sans contexte, la seconde confirmation est un état UI, la génération perd son sens ; contraire à la contrainte de conception |
44	| **B. Machine à états dans `netdiag`, primitives sans état dans `ports` (recommandée)** : `ports.Terminate`, `ports.Probe`, `ports.Kill` ; le modèle tient l'arrêt en cours, une chaîne de ticks sonde | Conforme à la contrainte (tick + sonde + génération) ; chaque primitive testable seule ; `ports` ne connaît ni l'UI ni le temps | Plus de messages côté UI |
45	
46	### 2.2 Envoyer SIGTERM
47	
48	| Option | Pour | Contre |
49	|---|---|---|
50	| **A. `realOS.kill(pid, want, sig)` reçoit le signal à envoyer (recommandée)** | Un seul point d'envoi, une seule vérification d'identité pour les deux signaux (critère 5) ; le garde statique et le garde à l'exécution restent **inchangés** (`p.Signal` et `p.Kill` dans `(realOS) kill`) | La méthode s'appelle toujours `kill` alors qu'elle peut envoyer SIGTERM (commentaire) |
51	| B. Une seconde méthode `realOS.term` | Nom exact | Deux points d'envoi : il faut changer `TestOnlyRealOSSendsASignal` (deux méthodes autorisées, deux gardes en tête) et dupliquer `FindProcess` + vérification ; le risque qu'une seule des deux vérifie grandit |
52	
53	### 2.3 Sonde « vivant / zombie / sorti »
54	
55	| Option | Pour | Contre |
56	|---|---|---|
57	| A. `kill(pid, 0)` / `p.Signal(0)` | Classique | Un signal (même nul) : le garde le refuse hors `realOS.kill` ; ne distingue pas le zombie (signal 0 réussit sur un zombie) ; ne voit pas un PID repris |
58	| B. Interroger le pidfd (`poll`) | Exact sous Linux ≥ 5.4 | Il faudrait tenir le pidfd pendant 5 s entre deux `Cmd` (état système hors modèle) ; rien sous macOS |
59	| **C. Lecture d'état sans signal, par PID, comparée à l'identité (recommandée)** : Linux `/proc/<pid>/stat` (état champ 3 + `starttime` champ 22 en une lecture) ; macOS `kinfo_proc` (`P_stat`, `P_starttime`) | Aucun signal ; détecte zombie **et** PID repris (identité différente = le processus visé est parti) ; réutilise `parseStartTicks` et le lecteur macOS existants | Une lecture par sonde ; macOS non exécuté en CI |
60	
61	### 2.4 Messages quand l'utilisateur quitte `:net`
62	
63	| Option | Pour | Contre |
64	|---|---|---|

93	
94	- **Un seul arrêt en attente** : `pm.stop *pendingStop` (nil = aucun). Phases `signalling`, `waiting`, `askingForce`, `forcing`. `pendingKill` reste la cible de la **première** confirmation (inchangé, Windows inclus).
95	- **Génération** : chaque arrêt reçoit `gen = nextStopGen()` (compteur `atomic.Uint64` de paquet, unique même entre deux modèles netdiag reconstruits). Tout message d'arrêt dont `gen` ≠ `pm.stop.gen`, ou reçu quand `pm.stop == nil`, ou dans une phase qui ne l'attend pas, est **ignoré** sans effet. `esc` met `pm.stop = nil` : le tick en vol devient périmé ; un nouvel arrêt lancé aussitôt a une autre génération, donc l'ancien tick ne le touche pas.
96	- **Échéance** : `deadline = msg.at + stopGrace`, `at` étant l'instant où le `Cmd` du SIGTERM a rendu ; chaque `portsStopProbeMsg` porte l'instant du tick (`tea.Tick` le fournit). Aucune horloge dans le modèle : les tests fixent `at`.
97	- **Sonde illisible** (erreur autre que « parti ») : journalisée, comptée **vivante** (aucune fausse annonce « stopped ») ; l'échéance amène la seconde confirmation, dont le SIGKILL revérifie l'identité.
98	- **Seconde étape** (`Yes`) : `targetPresence(target)` → `replaced` : `refusal(IdentityChangedError)` (critère 5, sans appel système) ; `absent` **n'arrête pas** la seconde étape (un processus qui s'arrête ferme souvent ses sockets avant de sortir ; c'est le cas même que la seconde étape doit traiter — l'identité est revérifiée au signal) ; protection recalculée ; puis SIGKILL par `pm.ops.kill(pid, target.Identity)`.
99	- **Résultat du SIGKILL d'un arrêt en deux temps** : `os.ErrProcessDone` → Info `x (N) stopped` (le processus est sorti de lui-même entre l'échéance et `Yes` ; décision proposée, plus juste que l'Error `PID N is no longer running`) ; `IdentityChangedError` → texte S-01b critère 2 + relecture (critère 5) ; le reste par `refusal` ; succès → Info `Process N terminated` (inchangé).
100	- **Pendant l'attente** : le tableau continue de se rafraîchir (chaîne `portsTickMsg` indépendante, la pause `space` reste un choix de l'utilisateur), toutes les touches répondent ; la chaîne de sonde n'est pas suspendue quand le terminal perd le focus (5 s bornées).
101	- **Windows** : `pm.stop` n'est **jamais** posé. `handleConfirmYes` garde exactement le chemin S-02a (`MarkBusy("Killing …")` + `killProcessCmd(kill, t, 0)`), sélectionné par `pm.ops.windows` (lui-même `runtime.GOOS == "windows"` en production, injecté en test). Aucune attente, aucune seconde confirmation, aucun texte nouveau.

335	
336	- **Rule 110** : `terminateCmd`, `stopProbeCmd`, `killProcessCmd` ne lisent pas le modèle ; toutes les transitions sont dans `Update`.

  holds no `spinner.Model` and no `spinner.TickMsg` handler.
- **The line spinner is gone**: `StatusColumn`, `portsSpinnerTickMsg`,
  `portsSpinnerCmd` and `handleSpinnerTick` are deleted. **State keeps its

  (`killFailureMessage`) and the row returns to rest: no `⊗`, nothing is

- **A periodic refresh never blinks**: `SetItems` leaves `busy` alone, so a

## The socket table — `internal/ports`

The machine's TCP and UDP sockets, and the process holding each, read **in this
process**. `List(ctx, resolve)`, `Kill(pid, Identity)`, `ConfirmIdentity(pid,
Identity)`, `Identity`, `ProtectionOf(pid)`, `Protection` (with `Reason()`),
`ProtectedError`, `UnverifiableError` and `IdentityChangedError` are the whole
interface (the two `...ForTest` constructors of `Identity` aside).

**It exists because the old one answered for the wrong machine** (D55). The
Ports tab ran `ss -tupan` inside
`docker run --rm --net=host --pid=host --privileged`, and on Docker Desktop
`--net=host` is the namespace of the Linux VM: the tab listed the VM's NFS
daemons with two-digit PIDs while not one of the host's 38 listening sockets
appeared, and `K` sent SIGKILL to a process of the VM under the impression it was
freeing a port on the machine. The sentence explaining this has sat at the top of
`docker.runDiagHost` since §3.33 rapatriated DNS, ICMP, TCP, TLS and HTTP for
exactly the same reason; `RunSS` and `KillProcess` were the two nobody pulled it
for. **Under Linux the defect did not exist**, which is why it went unnoticed:
the tab was right on the platform it was written on.
....
which only asks `Verifiable()`; `internal/ports` compares it (`Conflicts`: both
known and different). The zero value is "unknown", so a caller that forgets the
identity gets a refusal, not a signal. Three kinds exist: unknown, known, and
*deferred* (Windows only, below).

| OS | Where it is read | Raw value |
|---|---|---|
| Linux | `/proc/<pid>/stat`, field 22 (`starttime`), counted from the last `)` because the command name may contain spaces and parentheses (`parseStartTicks`) | ticks since boot |
| Windows | `GetProcessTimes`, `CreationTime` (`identity_windows.go`) | FILETIME as one 64-bit value (100 ns since 1601) |
| macOS | `sysctl kern.proc.pid`, `P_starttime` (`identity_darwin.go`) | seconds and microseconds as one value (`timevalStamp`) |
| other | nothing: the read returns `errors.ErrUnsupported` | every row unknown, `K` greyed |

- **Read once per distinct PID, at listing.** `List` calls `attachIdentities`
  after the socket snapshot. It reads each distinct PID once, in ascending
  order, and gives the value to every row of that PID. A PID that cannot be
  read leaves its rows unknown. `Socket.Identity` is not displayed.
  `ProtectionOf` and its `createTime` (milliseconds, from gopsutil) are
  untouched: the parent rule and the identity are two readings of two sources.
- **Windows: a budget, then a deferred read.** A creation time on Windows is a
  wall-clock time, so it can be compared with an instant. `List` takes `listedAt`
  *before* the snapshot, and a row counts as listed only if the process was
  created at least `windowsBirthSlack` (100 ms) before it (`judgeBirth`:
  `bornBefore`, `bornAround`, `bornAfter`); a process born later, or too close to
  tell, leaves the row unknown. Reading is capped at `windowsIdentityBudget`
  (100 ms) per refresh: when it runs out, the remaining PIDs get a *deferred*
  identity that carries `listedAt`, and `K` stays lit on them. The read happens
  when the confirmation opens (`ConfirmIdentity`, called by `confirmKill` in
  `Update`, so it is a short read at the press of `K`, never at render), with the
  same `judgeBirth` test: born before the listing gives a known identity, born
  after gives `IdentityChangedError`, too close to tell gives
  `UnverifiableError`. A deferred identity never reaches `Kill`: it is refused
  there as unverifiable. Linux and macOS have no budget; everything is read at
  listing.
- **Verified on the process held, then signalled.** `realOS.kill(pid, want)`
  opens the process with `os.FindProcess` (a pidfd on Linux 5.4 and later, a
  handle on Windows), reads the identity through that held process
  (`heldIdentity`, per OS), compares it with `want` (`verdictAtSignal`, a pure
  function) and only then calls `p.Kill()`, which signals through the same pidfd
  or handle. The PID cannot change hands between the comparison and the signal.
  A failed read never sends. The per-OS files contain no signalling call, so
  `TestOnlyRealOSSendsASignal` still holds.
- **Errors.** `UnverifiableError` (`Cannot verify which process PID N is — not
  stopped`) and `IdentityChangedError` (`PID N is no longer the process that was
  listed — not stopped`) are DevDesk's own refusals, like `ProtectedError`: they
  wrap no OS sentinel, so the screen never reads them as `Refused by the
  system`. `UnverifiableError.Cause` is for the log; `Unwrap` does not return it.
  An OS refusal (`os.ErrPermission`, for instance a Windows handle that cannot be
  opened) or a gone process (`os.ErrProcessDone`) stays readable through
  `errors.Is`, and `killFailureMessage` words it as before.
- **Order in `Kill`.** Parse, protection, `n <= 0`, then the identity: a
  non-known identity is an `UnverifiableError` and nothing is sent.

**Reaching the screen.** `PortsModel.refusal(pid, process, err)` is the one
classifier of every refused or failed stop: the press of `K` (the confirmation's
read), `Yes` (the table compared with the target) and the kill result all call
it. `errors.As` runs first for the three typed refusals; anything else goes
through `killFailureMessage` (`errors.Is`).

| Error | Footer | Level |
|---|---|---|
| `ProtectedError` | its own text | Warn |
| `IdentityChangedError` | `<name> (PID N) is no longer the process that was listed — table refreshed` (`PID N is …` when the name is empty), plus `requestPortsRefresh()` | Warn |
| `UnverifiableError` | its own text; the cause goes to the log | Warn |
| anything else | `killFailureMessage`: `Refused by the system — DevDesk cannot signal PID N`, `PID N is no longer running`, or the generic line | Error |

After an identity change the table is read once more, even when the tab is
paused (as `n` does), because the footer says it was refreshed; the pause stays
displayed.

**What is guaranteed, and what is not.**

- *Guaranteed*: on Linux with a pidfd, and on Windows within the assumptions
  below, no signal reaches a process other than the one whose identity was
  captured (at listing, or when the confirmation opened for a deferred row).
- *Residual windows, accepted and documented*:
  - **macOS, and Linux without a pidfd.** No handle on the process exists, so
    the comparison and the signal are two steps on a PID. `os.FindProcess` falls
    back to the bare PID, silently, on a kernel without the pidfd calls or where
    seccomp refuses them. The window is short, but it is there.
  - **Listing race (Linux, macOS).** The identity is read after the socket
    snapshot. If the holder exits and its PID is reused between the two, the row
    carries the newcomer's identity. That takes a full turn of `pid_max` within a
    few milliseconds. These stamps are not wall-clock times, so nothing compares
    them with an instant.
  - **Windows clock.** Anchoring to the listing instant assumes that
    `CreationTime` and `time.Now` read the same clock, with a granularity under
    100 ms (not verified). A wall clock set backwards
    between the listing and the read can make a younger process look older. A
    coarser granularity only produces cautious refusals (`bornAround`).
  - **Windows rows over the budget** are not greyed ahead of time when the system
    would refuse them: the refusal shows at the press of `K`. Reading PIDs in a
    stable order keeps the cut on the same PIDs from one refresh to the next.
  - **macOS `EIO`.** For a missing PID the kernel answers `sysctl kern.proc.pid`
    with no data, which `x/sys` reports as `EIO`. `readIdentity` reads `EIO`,
    `ESRCH`, `ENOENT` and a record with another `P_pid` as "process done"
    (not run on macOS).
- *Not run*: `identity_windows.go` and `identity_darwin.go` are compiled for
  their OS and read, never executed; no Windows or macOS machine was available.
  That `OpenProcess` with `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION` and the handle of
  `os.FindProcess` both allow `GetProcessTimes` is the documented behaviour of
  the API, not checked here.
- *Cost on Windows: not measured* (as of 2026-11-23). `windowsIdentityBudget` is
  the story's starting value, not a measured threshold. To measure it, on a
  Windows machine **without elevation**, with a busy socket table (the story's
  case is 189 sockets):
  `DEVDESK_MEASURE_IDENTITY=1 go test -run TestMeasureIdentityCost -v ./internal/ports`
  (PowerShell: set `$env:DEVDESK_MEASURE_IDENTITY=1` first). It reads the table
  and every distinct PID five times with no budget, and logs the sockets and PIDs
  counted, the failures by kind (permission, gone, other), the min, median and
  max per round, and the cost of `List`. It never signals. Write the result in a
  dated note under `docs/measurements/` and adjust the constant if it
  contradicts the budget (D175). The task is DEVDESK-727.

**The target is captured (DEVDESK-714).** `confirmKill` copies the selected
row's PID and process name into `pendingKill` (a `killTarget`) in `Update`,
and builds the text of the confirmation from it. `handleConfirmYes` reads
`pendingKill`, never the table: the refresh keeps running during the
confirmation and the table's cursor stays on an index, so the selected row can
be another process by the time the user answers. Before the bug, `Yes` stopped
that other process. `handleConfirmNo` and `handleConfirmYes` both clear
`pendingKill` and the modal; a `Yes` with no pending target does nothing.
The target also carries its `Identity`: the one the row was listed with, or the
one `ops.confirm` returned when the confirmation opened (a refusal there shows
at once and opens no modal). `handleConfirmYes` then, in this order:

1. `targetPresence`, which compares the target with the last table received
   without a system call and has three outcomes. `present`: a row of the same
   PID has the same name and no conflicting identity. `replaced`: a row of the
   same PID has a known identity that differs from the target's; nothing is
   sent, and `refusal` says the PID is no longer the process that was listed and
   reads the table again. `absent`: no such row; nothing is sent and the footer
   warns `<name> (PID N) is no longer listed — not stopped`. The process may be
   gone, or its PID may belong to another process now; a refusal costs the user
   one keypress, a wrong signal costs a process. A deferred or unknown identity
   never conflicts here (`Conflicts` needs both known); the signal verifies it.
2. `ops.protection` on the captured PID: a target that became protected since
   the confirmation opened is refused with a warning naming the reason.
3. The busy mark and `killProcessCmd(ops.kill, target)`, with `kill` and the
   target copied as values (Rule 110).

A `ProtectedError`, an `IdentityChangedError` or an `UnverifiableError` that
comes back from `Kill` (the in-depth refusal) shows as a footer **warning**, not
an error: a precondition was not met, nothing failed (Rule 128).

**Windows wording (DEVDESK-710).** Windows has no signal to send: the process
is ended at once through `TerminateProcess`. The confirmation says so and
promises nothing clean. `processOps.windows` selects the text; everything else
(title `Kill Process`, key `K`, one confirmation, `Killing <name> (<pid>)`,
`Process <pid> terminated`) is the same on every platform.

| | Linux, macOS | Windows |
|---|---|---|
| Body | `Send SIGKILL to <name> (PID <pid>)?` + `The process gets no chance to shut down cleanly.` | `Terminate <name> (PID <pid>)?` + `Windows has no clean stop for this process: it is ended at once and cannot save anything.` |
| Help for `K` | `Send SIGKILL to the selected process, after confirmation (Ports tab)` | `End the selected process at once, after confirmation (Ports tab)` |

A graceful close (`WM_CLOSE`) is a later story (S-04), not this one.

**Seams and the signal guard (DEVDESK-708, DEVDESK-709).**
`internal/ports/procos.go` holds the seams the package reads about the host:
`selfPID`, `parentPID`, `goos`, `now` (the listing instant and the Windows
budget) and `procOS` (an `osProcs` with `createTime`, `identity` and
`kill(pid, want)`; production value `realOS{}`). Per OS, `identity_linux.go`,
`identity_windows.go`, `identity_darwin.go` and `identity_other.go` hold
`readIdentity`, `heldIdentity` and `isNoSuchProcess`. In `netdiag`, `processOps`
(`protection`, `confirm`, `kill`, `windows`) gathers what the tab asks of the
system, wired by `realProcessOps()` to `ports.ProtectionOf`,
`ports.ConfirmIdentity`, `ports.Kill` and `runtime.GOOS == "windows"`; tests
replace `PortsModel.ops`, so no netdiag test can reach `ports.Kill`. A test
builds an identity with `ports.IdentityForTest(raw)` or
`ports.DeferredIdentityForTest(listedAt)`; both panic outside a test binary.

`realOS.kill` is the **only** place in the package that sends a signal, and its
first statement is `refuseRealSignalUnderTest`: in a test binary
(`testing.Testing()`), a real signal **panics** unless the test called
`allowRealSignals(t)`. It panics rather than returning an error because an
error looks like an ordinary failed kill and the test could still pass. Two
tests hold the guard:

- `TestARealSignalInATestBinaryPanics` and
  `TestKillWithoutASubstitutedProcOSHitsTheGuard` run the panic.
- `TestOnlyRealOSSendsASignal` parses the non-test files of `internal/ports`
  and fails on a signalling call (`os.FindProcess`, `syscall.Kill`,
  `unix.Kill`, `windows.TerminateProcess`, a `.Kill(` or `.Signal(` method)
  outside `(realOS) kill`, or if the guard is not its first statement. It does
  not see an aliased import, another package or an external binary.

Two tests send a real signal, each to a child the test started itself:
`TestKillEndsARealChildProcess` and `TestKillSparesARealChildWhoseIdentityDiffers`
(the child must survive: the identity differs, so nothing is sent).
`TestKillOfAnExitedChildSendsNothing` calls `Kill` on a child that already
exited. They re-run the test binary as a child (`TestHelperProcessSleeps`), call
`allowRealSignals(t)` and wait for it. Never call
`allowRealSignals` in a test aimed at anything else. The seams are globals:
no `t.Parallel` in the package.

**Known limits.** S-01b (DEVDESK-709) closed the PID-reuse window on Linux with
a pidfd and on Windows with a handle. What stays, said plainly (the guarantees
and the cost measurement are under « Process identity »):

1. **macOS, and Linux without a pidfd** (kernel older than 5.4, or seccomp
   filtering `pidfd_open`). `os.FindProcess` silently falls back to the bare
   PID, so the comparison and the signal are two steps on a PID. The window is a
   few microseconds, and using it would need a whole turn of `pid_max` at an
   identical tick: impractical, not impossible.
2. **Identity read after the snapshot (Linux, macOS).** `attachIdentities` runs
   after the socket snapshot; a PID that changes hands in those few
   milliseconds carries the newcomer's identity.
3. **Windows clock set backwards.** `judgeBirth` compares a creation time with
   the listing instant (`windowsBirthSlack`, 100 ms). If the clock goes back
   between the listing and the birth of a process that took the PID, the
   newcomer can look older than the listing. It applies to both read paths; it
   matters mostly for a deferred row, where the gap lasts until the
   confirmation opens.
4. **`HOST_PROC`.** gopsutil pairs sockets and PIDs under that prefix, but
   `readIdentity` reads `/proc` as a literal path and the pidfd acts in
   DevDesk's own PID namespace. If `HOST_PROC` points at another namespace's
   `/proc`, the check agrees with itself and cannot see the mismatch. This
   predates S-01b.
5. **Windows inherited sockets.** A socket inherited by a child can keep the
   `OwningPid` of a parent that exited, with that PID reused before the listing.
   The identity is read from the PID as listed, so it matches the newcomer and
   the row is not caught. This predates S-01b.
6. **Windows and macOS code never ran.** `identity_windows.go` and
   `identity_darwin.go` are compiled and vetted, not executed. Unconfirmed
   assumptions: an unknown PID fails `OpenProcess` (and `os.FindProcess`) with
   `ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER` on Windows; a missing PID answers `EIO`, or a record
   whose `P_pid` differs, on macOS.

Also: the process name in the footer comes from the system and is not
sanitised (DEVDESK-720). `targetPresence` trusts the last table received: a
paused or stale table is trusted as it stands, and the signal is what verifies.
`createTime` (milliseconds) still feeds the parent rule and `Identity` is a
second source; unifying them would change S-01a and is not done. When
`parentPID()` is 0 (PID namespace), the parent is not protected.

The platform error never reaches the screen — measured, PID 4 on this machine
answers `OpenProcess: Accès refusé.`, in the machine's own language, which is

otherwise re-attempt every one of those lookups on every refresh tick — the
exact kind of request storm the cache exists to prevent, just arriving
through failed lookups instead of successful ones.

### The dot while `K` runs

The leftmost column of the Ports table is empty at rest. After you confirm `K`, every socket of that process shows a blinking dot (`●` / `○`) until the system answers, and the footer reads `Killing sshd (812)` for the selected row. The State cell keeps its text, dimmed. If the system refuses, the footer says so and the dot goes away: a failed kill leaves no mark on the row. The periodic refresh never makes a dot blink. Press `?` for the legend.

A network test that fails (TCP refused, invalid TLS) is a result, not a failed operation: it stays in the Verdict column of the Diagnostics tab.

On a narrow terminal whole columns drop, rightmost first: Process under 103 columns, then PID under 91, then Peer Address under 82, down to Proto, State and Local Address from 54.

### Killing a process

Signaling a process uses whatever rights the DevDesk process itself has —
which means killing another user's process, or a system service, now
correctly comes back as "refused by the operating system" instead of
silently succeeding against the wrong machine (as it effectively did when
run inside a privileged, host-networked container).

Because the operating system's refusal is only knowable after the attempt,
the UI treats these questions differently:

- **No PID means the action is unavailable before you even try** — a socket
  the OS won't attribute to a process has the kill shortcut visibly
  disabled on that row, rather than appearing available and failing with an
  explanation only after the keypress.
- **Some processes are protected, and the key is disabled on them too.**
  DevDesk refuses to stop itself, the process that started it (its direct
  parent), and PID 1. On Windows it also refuses PIDs 0 and 4. On such a row
  the kill shortcut is greyed out, and pressing `K` puts the reason in the
  footer: `This is DevDesk itself`, `This process started DevDesk`,
  `PID 1 is the system's init process` or `Windows system process`. This is
  DevDesk's own rule, not a guess about what the OS would allow. Only the
  direct parent is protected: a terminal or a multiplexer further up is not.
  If DevDesk cannot read when its parent was created, it protects the parent.
- **Some rows cannot be checked, and the key is disabled on them.** Before it
  stops anything, DevDesk wants to be sure that a PID still belongs to the
  process you saw. When it could not read what it needs to tell, the kill
  shortcut is greyed out and pressing `K` puts `Cannot verify which process
  this is` in the footer. The row stays visible. DevDesk's own rows keep their
  own reason (`This is DevDesk itself`).
- **Whether the OS actually accepts the signal is answered by the attempt,
  not predicted in advance** — a row with a real PID stays enabled even
  when the kill is likely to be refused, since guessing at permissions
  ahead of time can be wrong in both directions. The resulting error is
  classified rather than shown as a raw platform error string: a permission
  failure reads as "refused by the system," a process that already exited
  reads as "no longer running," and anything else falls back to a generic
  message.

### What the confirmation stops

The confirmation names a process and its PID, for example
`Send SIGKILL to node (PID 4242)?`. Confirming stops **that** process, even
if the table has refreshed and moved since you pressed `K`. The text does not
change while the confirmation is open, and answering No or pressing `esc` sends
nothing.

If the process is no longer in the table when you confirm, DevDesk stops
nothing and the footer says `node (PID 4242) is no longer listed — not stopped`.
The process may have exited, and its PID may now belong to another process.
Press `K` again on the row you want.

### What DevDesk checks before it stops anything

A PID is only a number. When a process exits, the system can give its number to
a new, unrelated process. So DevDesk remembers which process each row was when
the table was read, and checks, at the moment it sends the signal, that the PID
still belongs to that process. If it does not, nothing is sent. The footer says:

```text
node (PID 4242) is no longer the process that was listed — table refreshed
```

and the table is read again, even if you paused it. Press `K` on the row you
want from the new table. If the process has no name, the message starts with
`PID 4242`.

Two other messages come from the same check:

- `Cannot verify which process PID 4242 is — not stopped` means DevDesk lost the
  means to tell, so it did not guess.
- `Refused by the system — DevDesk cannot signal PID 4242` means the operating
  system itself said no. On Windows this can also appear as soon as you press `K`, on a
  row that was lit: DevDesk then checks that row at that moment instead of when
  the table was read, and the system may refuse.

On Linux the check and the signal go to the same process handle, so the PID
cannot change hands between them. On macOS, and on a Linux kernel or sandbox
without that support, a very short gap remains between the check and the
signal. On Windows the check compares the process's creation time with the
moment the table was read, which assumes the computer's clock did not jump
backwards in between.

On Windows there is no way to ask a process to close cleanly from here. The
confirmation reads `Terminate node.exe (PID 4412)?` and says that the process
is ended at once and cannot save anything. On Linux and macOS the process gets
a SIGKILL, which does not let it shut down cleanly either.

## Cross-View Communication

Key messages in `internal/app/messages.go`:
- `SwitchViewMsg` — navigate to another view
- `SelectionRequestMsg` / `SelectionResultMsg` — selection mode (e.g., workspaces opened from security view to pick a repo)
- `ImageScanResultLoadedMsg` / `WorkspaceScanResultLoadedMsg` — cached results ready

### Long-running work reports without taking the screen

A scan, a sync or a delete outlives the moment the user spends looking at the
view that started it. Its progress messages are therefore addressed **by name**
to that view — `routeToView(target, msg)` in `app.go` — and never to the view on
screen, and routing one never changes `currentView`.

Three properties, and each is load-bearing:

| | |
|---|---|
| The owning view is updated | it holds the row's marker, its footer state and its cache write; a message dropped because the user walked away leaves the row marked busy for the life of the view |
| The active view is *not* | it would act on progress that is not its own |
| `currentView` is untouched | `handleWorkspaceScanComplete` used to set it on every finished repository, so a batch of twelve made every other view unusable until the last one landed (D67) |

The router does not re-measure the layout on these, unlike
`forwardToActiveView`: a view the user is not looking at cannot change the
footer's shape on screen, and it is measured on its way back in — `switchView`
asks for a resize.

Making the marker survive re-entry is what makes the routing safe: `setEntries`
deliberately does not touch `scanningPaths`, so the reload `Init` triggers on
the way back in leaves in-flight work alone.

new='''**Two-step stop (DEVDESK-711, S-02b).** On Linux and macOS `K` asks for a clean
stop first and forces only after a second confirmation. `internal/ports` holds
stateless primitives; the state machine lives in `internal/ui/netdiag`
(`ports_stop.go`), because the wait must not block and `esc` must be able to end
it (Rule 110).

- **Primitives (`internal/ports`).** `Terminate(pid, Identity)` sends SIGTERM and
  returns at once; it waits for nothing. `Kill` is unchanged (SIGKILL,
  `TerminateProcess` on Windows). Both call `signalTarget` and then the single
  `procOS.kill(pid, want, sig)`, so protection, identity and the held process
  are the same for both signals. `Terminate` wraps its error `stopping process
  N: %w`; `refusal` reads it with `errors.As` and `errors.Is`, so the prefix
  never reaches the screen. On Windows `Terminate` answers `ErrNoCleanStop`,
  after the protection check; the UI never calls it there.
- **The probe sends nothing.** `Probe(pid, Identity)` reads the state and the
  identity stamp in one read (`readStatus`: `/proc/<pid>/stat` on Linux,
  `sysctl kern.proc.pid` on macOS) and decides in `livenessOf`:
  `ProcessExited` when no process holds the PID **or when another process does**
  (the stamp differs from the listed one: the listed process is gone),
  `ProcessZombie` (state `Z` or `X` on Linux, `P_stat == 5` on macOS, local
  constant `darwinSZOMB` since `x/sys` exports none), else `ProcessRunning`.
  `Liveness.Stopped()` is true for the first two. A read that fails for another
  reason returns `ProcessRunning` with the error: an unreadable probe is never
  taken for a stop. On Windows and other platforms `Probe` returns

  no wait, through `refusal` (the same classifier as before: `Refused by the
  system — DevDesk cannot signal PID N`, `PID N is no longer running`, the

EOF

result, one probe per 250 ms tick, the SIGKILL result. They must reach netdiag
whether or not `:net` is on screen, or the chain stops when the user leaves, `K`
stays greyed and the row stays busy.

The rule: a message type that belongs to such a chain implements
`netdiag.BackgroundMsg` (an interface with one unexported method, so only
netdiag's own types can). `App.update` has one case for it, before `default`, and
`routeNetdiagWork` does the rest:

| `:net` is | The message goes to |
|---|---|
| on screen | the active view, as any other message (`forwardToActiveView`) |
| off screen | the netdiag view the router holds, through `routeToView`: `currentView` is untouched and the layout is not re-measured |
| not open at all | nowhere: no view is created for it |

Only netdiag's own types implement the interface
(`TestOnlyNetdiagWorkIsBackgroundMessage` checks that a key, a resize, a ports
read and an unrelated message do not), so no message the router already routes by
another rule is redirected. A view that uses this road must also report
`Running()` while the chain lives; netdiag does while a stop is pending, so
naming it again from the command line does not rebuild it
(`TestNamingNetdiagDoesNotDropAStopInFlight`). What the stop does is in
`network.md`, « Two-step stop ».

### The jobs registry — `internal/jobs`"""

open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

Rejected: dropping them (`K` greyed for good, row busy for good) and re-arming in `Init` (the SIGTERM result would be unknowable, the chain could double). (5) Every message carries the generation of its stop (package atomic counter): `esc`, a refused signal or a new stop makes the tick still in flight stale, and it is ignored. (6) The deadline is the instant the SIGTERM returned plus 5 s, compared with the tick instant: no clock in the model. (7) An unreadable probe is logged and counts as running: nothing is announced that was not seen. (8) The second `Yes` uses the identity captured at the first confirmation and recomputes the protection; a `replaced` row is refused with no system call, an `absent` one is not (a stopping process often closes its sockets before it exits); the SIGKILL verifies the identity again. (9) Windows is unchanged: `pm.stop` is never set, one confirmation, `Killing …`, `Process N terminated`; `Terminate` answers `ErrNoCleanStop`, `Probe` `errors.ErrUnsupported`, and the UI calls neither. Limits and risks: not run on macOS (`kern.proc.pid` on a zombie, `P_stat == SZOMB`, a constant copied from `<sys/proc.h>`, not verified; if the kernel does not return it the read is « gone » and the stop counts either way; SIP may refuse SIGTERM); the second confirmation can open while the user is on another tab or view and is not visible there; rebuilding the netdiag view during the wait loses it (`Running()` protects only a view opened from another view); the 5 s window of PID reuse is covered by the identity stamp, with the residual window of D175 at each signal; the second `Yes` relies on the identity check at the signal alone for an absent row. Known bug, not fixed here: the Windows confirmation of S-02a (a line of 89 cells) overflows an 80-column terminal, DEVDESK-735. No ADR: local, reversible by a revert, no schema, cache or configuration. **Plane:** DEVDESK-711; bug DEVDESK-735. Number: D175 is the highest in this worktree; re-check at merge. Sources: `internal/ports/{ports,probe,procos,identity,identity_*}.go`, `internal/ui/netdiag/{ports_stop,ports_model,ports_commands,header,update}.go`, `internal/app/app.go`, `docs/architecture/network.md` (« Two-step stop »), `docs/architecture/app-shell.md`.**

"""

open(p,'w').write(s)

p='docs/journal.md'
s=open(p).read()
anchor="## 2026-11-23 — Safe process stop: S-01b delivered"
assert s.count(anchor)==1
e="""## 2026-11-23 — Safe process stop: S-02b delivered, ask to stop first, force on a second confirmation (DEVDESK-711)

Source: `docs/product/safe-process-stop/stories.md`; `docs/architecture/network.md` (« Two-step stop »); decision D176 in `docs/backlog.md`. Plane: DEVDESK-711; bug DEVDESK-735.

1. **Delivered (Linux, macOS):** `K` asks `Ask <name> (PID N) to stop?`, sends SIGTERM and watches the process for up to 5 s without blocking the screen. If it leaves (a zombie counts), the footer says `<name> (N) stopped`. If not, a `Force Kill` confirmation offers SIGKILL; nothing is forced without it. `esc` stops waiting and takes nothing back. Windows is unchanged: one confirmation, the process is ended at once.
2. **Decided (orchestrator, within the autonomy the user granted on 2026-11-23; the user can overrule):** the 5 s is fixed; `K` reads `Stop process` on Linux and macOS and `Kill process` on Windows; a zombie counts as stopped; one stop at a time. The Rule 130 exception (`K` greyed during a stop) is written in D176.
3. **Also:** results and ticks of a stop reach netdiag when `:net` is off screen (`netdiag.BackgroundMsg`), which fixes a kill result lost the same way.
4. **Limits:** not run on macOS (zombie read unverified); the second confirmation is not visible off the Ports tab; rebuilding the view loses the wait.
5. **Open:** the Windows confirmation of S-02a overflows 80 columns (DEVDESK-735).

"""

open(p,'w').write(s)
